title: Graceful shutdown and where to go next
summary: Implementing Drop for the ThreadPool, the cannot-move-out-of-a-mutable-reference error and Vec::drain, closing the channel with Option::take so workers leave their loops, the final server that stops after two requests, keeping workers alive when a job panics, and ideas for taking the project and your Rust further.

sections: TRPL 21.3 Implementing the Drop Trait on ThreadPool
TRPL 21.3 Signaling to the Threads to Stop Listening for Jobs

blocks.md: The pool works, but stopping it is crude: Ctrl-C kills the process, and every thread dies on the spot, even one halfway through writing a response. A **graceful shutdown** lets each worker finish the job it has, then stop, and the program waits for all of them. In Rust the natural place for cleanup is **`Drop`** (chapter 15): when the `ThreadPool` goes out of scope, it should join its threads.

blocks.title: First attempt: join in Drop
blocks.md: `JoinHandle::join` takes `self`, it consumes the handle. But `drop` only gets `&mut self`, so iterating gives `&mut Worker`, and we cannot move the handle out from behind a mutable reference:

blocks.output:
error[E0507]: cannot move out of `worker.thread` which is behind a mutable reference
  --> src/main.rs:16:13
   |
16 |             worker.thread.join().unwrap();
   |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ------ `worker.thread` moved due to this method call
   |             |
   |             move occurs because `worker.thread` has type `JoinHandle<()>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
   |
note: `JoinHandle::<T>::join` takes ownership of the receiver `self`, which moves `worker.thread`
  --> /rustc/2d8144b7880597b6e6d3dfd63a9a9efae3f533d3/library/std/src/thread/join_handle.rs:149:16
blocks.explain: The compiler even suggests the classic fix: wrap the handle in an `Option` and `take()` it. The book prefers not to, because then every other use of `thread` has to deal with an `Option` that is only ever `None` during drop.

blocks.title: Closing the channel
blocks.md: When every `Sender` is dropped, the channel is closed and `recv` returns `Err`. So `Drop` first drops the pool's sender, then joins the workers, and each worker leaves its loop when `recv` fails. To move the sender out of `&mut self`, the pool stores it as **`Option<Sender<Job>>`** and calls `take()`; here an `Option` is the right tool, because the sender really does go away while the pool still exists. The order inside `drop` matters: drop the sender first, or the joins wait forever.

blocks.output:
queued 8 jobs, finished so far: 0
after the pool is dropped: 8
blocks.explain: Jobs already in the channel are still delivered after the sender is dropped; `recv` only fails once the queue is empty. So dropping the pool finishes all queued work, not just the jobs in progress.

blocks.title: The finished server
blocks.md: To see the shutdown happen, the book makes `main` accept only two requests, with `listener.incoming().take(2)`. After the loop, `pool` goes out of scope and `Drop` runs. With the book's messages added to the worker and to `drop`, the whole program is:

blocks.explain: This is the book's final `main.rs`; the library is the pool above, with `println!("Worker {id} got a job; executing.")` in the worker, `println!("Worker {id} disconnected; shutting down.")` before its `break`, and `println!("Shutting down worker {}", worker.id)` in `drop`. It needs `hello.html` and `404.html` next to `Cargo.toml` and a browser, so run it on your own machine.

blocks.md: Making two requests prints something like the following. The order varies from run to run, because the four workers are real threads; the shape does not: two jobs are executed, `Shutting down.` appears when `main` leaves the loop, every worker reports that its channel closed, and every worker is joined.

Shutting down.

blocks.explain: Worker 3 took the second request while `main` was already waiting to join worker 0: shutdown does not cut off work in progress.

blocks.title: One more failure mode: panicking jobs
blocks.md: If a job panics, the panic unwinds through the worker's loop and that thread dies; the pool silently gets smaller, and when the last worker dies, queued jobs are never run. Worse, a panic while a worker holds the `Mutex` poisons it, and every other worker's `lock().unwrap()` panics too. Since our worker releases the lock before running the job, poisoning cannot happen here, and running each job inside `std::panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(job))` keeps the worker alive. The exercise asks for exactly that.

blocks.title: Wait for the workers
blocks.md: This pool has no `Drop`, so `main` reads the counter as soon as the pool goes out of scope, while the workers are still busy. Implement `Drop for ThreadPool`: close the channel with `self.sender.take()`, then join every worker taken out with `self.workers.drain(..)`.
hints: `impl Drop for ThreadPool { fn drop(&mut self) { ... } }`
Drop the sender before joining: `drop(self.sender.take());` then `for worker in self.workers.drain(..) { worker.join().unwrap(); }`.

blocks.title: A pool that shuts down cleanly and survives panics
blocks.goal: Finish the thread pool: graceful shutdown in Drop, an explicit shutdown, counters, and workers that keep going when a job panics.
blocks.behavior:
- `ThreadPool::new(size)` panics for 0.
- `execute(&self, f) -> Result<(), PoolClosed>`: queues the job, or returns `Err(PoolClosed)` after `shutdown`.
- Every job runs inside `catch_unwind`, so a panicking job does not kill its worker. `completed()` counts jobs that returned normally and `panicked()` counts jobs that panicked.
- `shutdown(&mut self)`: close the channel and join every worker, so every job queued before the call has finished when it returns. Calling it twice is fine.
- `join(self) -> (usize, usize)`: shut down and return `(completed, panicked)`.
- `Drop` shuts down the same way.

examples.input: pool of 2; 3 jobs that panic and 5 that return; pool.join()

hints: Share two `Arc<AtomicUsize>` counters with the workers.
Inside the worker: `match panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(job)) { Ok(()) => completed.fetch_add(1, ...), Err(_) => panicked.fetch_add(1, ...) };`.
`shutdown`: `drop(self.sender.take());` then join everything from `self.workers.drain(..)`. Both are no-ops the second time.
`join(mut self)` can call `self.shutdown()` and then read the counters; `Drop` still runs afterwards and does nothing.
blocks.solution_explain: `shutdown` is idempotent because both `Option::take` and `drain` leave nothing behind, so `join` and `Drop` can share it. `catch_unwind` turns a job's panic into a value, which keeps the worker looping; `AssertUnwindSafe` is needed because a boxed `FnOnce` is not known to be unwind-safe, and it is fine here since the job's state is gone after a panic. The lock is released before the job runs, so a panic can never poison it.

blocks.title: Where to go from here
blocks.md:
The book closes with ideas for improving the server, each a good exercise in a part of this course:

- Add documentation to `ThreadPool` and its public methods, and tests of the library (chapters 11 and 14).
- Replace the `unwrap` calls with real error handling (chapter 9), and handle a client that sends garbage (you did in the first exercise).
- Use the pool for something other than web requests.
- Compare with production crates: **`rayon`** for data-parallel thread pools, **`tokio`** and **`axum`** or **`hyper`** for async servers that handle tens of thousands of connections (chapter 17), and **`signal-hook`** to shut down on Ctrl-C (chapter 24).

*Comprehensive Rust*'s idiomatic-Rust day adds habits worth keeping: run **`cargo clippy`** and **`rustfmt`** on every project, follow the **Rust API Guidelines** for naming and conversions (`new`, `build`, `as_`, `to_`, `into_`), make invalid states unrepresentable with types (chapters 5, 18 and 24), and prefer returning `Result` to panicking in libraries.

You started this course with `println!("Hello, world!")`. You can now read and write ownership-checked code, model data with enums and traits, write tests, build concurrent and async programs, use unsafe code and FFI responsibly, and work below the standard library. The best next step is a project of your own.

questions.q: Why does `worker.thread.join()` fail to compile inside `drop(&mut self)` when iterating `&mut self.workers`?
options: join takes the handle by value, and we only have a mutable reference
questions.explanation: drain(..) gives the workers by value.

questions.q: Why must `drop` drop the sender before joining?
options: Otherwise workers wait on recv forever and join never returns
questions.explanation: Closing the channel makes recv return Err.

questions.q: After the sender is dropped, what happens to jobs still in the channel?
options: They are still received and run; recv fails only when the queue is empty
They run on the main thread

questions.q: Why is the sender stored as `Option<Sender<Job>>`?
options: So Drop can move it out with take() while the pool still exists

questions.q: What keeps a worker alive when a job panics?
questions.explanation: The panic becomes an Err value.

points: Graceful shutdown belongs in Drop: close the channel, then join every worker.
join consumes the handle; Vec::drain(..) hands out workers by value from &mut self.
Store the sender as Option and take() it; recv returns Err once the channel is closed and empty.
Release the lock before running a job, and run jobs inside catch_unwind so a panic cannot kill or poison the pool.
Next: rayon, tokio and axum in practice, clippy and rustfmt always, and a project of your own.

terms.def: Stopping a program by letting work in progress finish and releasing resources, instead of killing it.
A method that removes a range of elements from a vector and yields them by value.
Moves the value out of an Option, leaving None in its place.
Runs a closure and turns a panic inside it into an Err value.
